metadata.title: Charaka Samhita - Nidana Sthana, Vimana Sthana, Sharira Sthana
metadata.description: Comprehensive knowledge base of Charaka Samhita's diagnostic principles, specific medical principles, and human constitution chapters

sthanas.description: The second section within Charak Samhita, dealing with guidelines for diagnosing disease on the basis of detailed history and clinical examination. The term Nidana literally means primary cause and diagnosis.

chapters.summary: The first chapter introduces fundamental principles of diagnosis and fever (jwara). The first part deals with necessary tools for acquiring comprehensive knowledge of any disease - Nidana Panchaka (five diagnostic tools): etiology (hetu), premonitory signs (purvarupa), clinical features (rupa), pacifying factors (upashaya), and pathogenesis (samprapti). The second part applies these tools to explain fever and its types (endogenous and exogenous). Jwara is caused by accumulation of vitiated dosha at the site of digestion and further affliction of digestion and thermal regulation. It is considered both an independent ailment and a secondary condition of other diseases, and also an etiology responsible for various diseases.
importantVerses: Jwara afflicts the body, senses and the mind, is the first disease to be manifested, and is the principal and the most powerful disease.
Amashaya (stomach) is common to all types of jwara.
Pathogenetic dosha combined with heat located in amashaya and accompanying rasa obstructs the passage of rasa and sweda, causing them to spread all over the body.

chapters.summary: This chapter deals with diagnosis of bleeding disorders (raktapitta) caused by excess of pitta dosha vitiating blood tissue (rakta dhatu). This leads to capillary breakdown causing hemorrhage from external openings like mouth, per rectum, nose, eyes, ears, urethra. Contributing factors include consumption of incompatible food, certain meats with alcohol, butter milk with meat. Vitiated pitta has same color and smell as rakta dhatu and blends seamlessly with it. The pathogenesis differs based on associated dosha - if associated with kapha, bleeding occurs from upper orifices; if with vata, from lower orifices.
keyConcepts: Pitta dosha and rakta dhatu relationship
importantVerses: Raktapitta manifests through two broadly divided routes - upper tract and lower tract.
Raktapitta from upper orifices is curable, while from lower orifices is palliative.
Manifestation of bleeding from both tracts is said to be incurable.

chapters.summary: The third chapter describes etiology, pathogenesis, clinical features and therapeutics of lumps in abdomen. Gulma is a growth that could occur anywhere in the body, primarily caused by vitiated vata. The description denotes localized intra-abdominal swellings of multiple origin. In patients weakened by diseases or cleansing therapies, or suffering from stressful conditions, vata gets vitiated and enters mahasrotas causing formation of gulma. There are five types: four common to both males and females, and one (raktaja gulma) limited to females in uterine region.
importantVerses: Gulma is a disease of mahasrotas caused due to predominance of vata.
Sannipatika gulma is incurable, rest four are curable when treated timely.
Vata gets vitiated by two basic means - dhatukshaya (tissue wasting) and margavarana (obstruction).

chapters.summary: This chapter describes Prameha (obstinate urinary disorders including diabetes), its etiopathogenesis, types, clinical features, prognosis, prodromal symptoms, complications and line of treatment. Though predominantly a kapha dosha disorder, there are variants involving all three doshas and ten dushya. Excessive and turbid urination are cardinal signs. The chapter explains interaction of exogenous factors, endogenous and tissue response factors in disease manifestation. Twenty types are described: ten curable kaphaja, six palliative, and four incurable vataja.
importantVerses: Excessive and turbid urination are the cardinal signs of all prameha.
Vitiated kapha affects ten fluid-predominant body tissues, resulting in production of excessive kleda.
Manifestation of disease depends upon interaction between causative factors, dosha, dushya and defense mechanism.

chapters.summary: This chapter deals with diagnosis of skin disease termed Kushtha. The disease has variable manifestations on skin depending upon degree of involvement of three vitiated dosha and their effect on four vitiated factors (rasa, rakta, mamsa, lasika). On basis of clinical manifestations and severity, Kushtha is classified into seven major types, eleven minor types or innumerable types. The chapter covers etiopathology, prodromal symptoms, symptomatology of seven major types, dosha predominance, prognosis, complications and significance of early treatment.
keyConcepts: Four vitiated dhatus (tvak, rakta, mamsa, lasika)
importantVerses: Pathology of skin diseases originates from deranged physiology of seven factors - vata, pitta, kapha doshas and tvak, mamsa, shonita, lasika.
Kushtha is result of combined and simultaneous involvement of all three dosha and vitiation of four body constituents.
Seven mahakushtha and eleven kshudrakushtha are described.

chapters.summary: This chapter describes basics of etiopathogenesis of progressive wasting disease termed Shosha and its culmination in Rajayakshma (pulmonary tuberculosis). Shosha is characterized by severe depletion of tissues (phthisis). Four primary causes: overexertion (sahasa), suppression of natural urges (vegavidharana), pre-existing emaciation (kshaya), and wrong dietary habits (vishamashana). These lead to progressive loss of strength, vitiating three doshas and culminating in Rajayakshma.
importantVerses: There are four causes of shosha: overexertion, suppression of urges, wasting, and irregular consumption of improper food articles.
Shosha is different from kshataksheena - a post-treatment stage of localized or generalized emaciation.
Shosha and kshaya can be considered as independent clinical entities warranting independent strategies.

chapters.summary: This chapter describes detailed etiopathogenesis and types of major mental disorders named Unmada. The word literally means frenzy, madness or mental derangement. Characterized by disordered mental state in faculties of mind and intellect, leading to perverted thought processes, decision making, intellectual functioning, orientation, responsiveness, memory, desires, habits, character, psychomotor activity, conduct and behaviour. Unmada is classified into two broad categories: nija (endogenous - vata, pitta, kapha, sannipataja) and agantu (exogenous).
importantVerses: Unmada covers a wide range of major mental disorders and is synonymous with madness and mental derangement.
Patient develops derangement of all activities of manas, buddhi, ahamkara and indriyas.
When doshas move upwards into the head, they cause aberrations in functioning of manas producing mada.

chapters.summary: This chapter deals with psychiatric disorder leading to transient loss of consciousness termed Apasmara. It describes causative factors, predisposing conditions, pathogenesis, signs, types and prognosis. The clinical presentation simulates seizure disorders. Apasmara is a neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by intermittent loss of consciousness, memory, abnormal movements and blackouts. The chapter explores principles of psychiatric disorders involving memory, mind, consciousness and intellect. It also deals with Nidanarthakara roga - how one disease triggers another.
importantVerses: Apasmara simulates epilepsy in its features.
Ayurveda emphasizes heart as core pathological site while covering diseases of memory, intellect and psyche.
Vitiated doshas get through vessels of heart and move upwards to brain, afflicting senses and altering memory.

sthanas.description: Vimana Sthana is about quantification of vitiation of dosha and other specific factors responsible for causing disease or impairing health. It describes dietary regulations, causes of epidemics, basic body systems, acquiring knowledge of disease and patient, and medical education.

chapters.summary: The chapter deals with taste (rasa) and its importance in diet related to health. There are six rasas: madhura (sweet), amla (sour), lavana (saline), katu (pungent), tikta (bitter), and kashaya (astringent). These have pacifying and provoking effects on physiological status of dosha due to conjunction of rasas and dosha by virtue of their similar and dissimilar properties. Eight specific factors of dieting and twelve guidelines about eating food are described.
keyConcepts: Madhura (sweet) - aggravates kapha, pacifies vata and pitta
Amla (sour) - aggravates pitta and kapha, pacifies vata
Katu (pungent) - aggravates vata and pitta, pacifies kapha
importantVerses: Rasas are six - sweet, sour, saline, pungent, bitter and astringent.
Three rasa aggravate one dosha, whereas others pacify it.
Proportionate use of all six rasas in diet is considered healthy practice.

chapters.summary: This chapter deals with classification of individuals based on the type of abdomen (kukshi) and their digestive capacity. The three types help in determining dietary and therapeutic approaches. It provides knowledge about different body constitutions and their response to treatment.

This chapter deals with prevention of various epidemic disorders caused due to polluted air, water, soil and season. The contamination of these four factors is basic cause of higher mortality rate in an area. The four main environmental factors: vayu (air), jala (water), desha (land) and kaala (season) cause epidemic situations. Root cause of vitiation is adharma (unrighteousness) and prajnaparadha (intellectual error).
importantVerses: The common factors which affect mass population are vayu, jala, desha and kaala.
Root cause of vitiation of these factors is adharma and prajnaparadha.
When righteous acts disappear, seasons get impaired, air does not blow properly, land is afflicted, water reservoirs dry up.

chapters.summary: This chapter describes three methods for knowledge of disease - Trividha Pariksha. The three methods are: Aptopadesha (authoritative knowledge from scriptures), Pratyaksha (direct observation), and Anumana (inference). These methods are essential for proper clinical examination of patient and disease diagnosis.
importantVerses: One should examine various aspects of diseases by employing all three pramanas.
Observations made on nature of disease thereafter are infallible.
All three methods of examination are always to be used in sequence.

chapters.summary: This chapter provides detailed description of srotas (transportation and perfusion channels) in the body. Thirteen gross channels are clinically approachable: three channels for intake (pranavaha, udakavaha, annavaha), three for excretion (purishavaha, mutravaha, swedavaha), and seven for dhatu sustenance (rasavaha, raktavaha, mamsavaha, medovaha, asthivaha, majjavaha, shukravaha). Each channel has pair of base organs. Ama is most common cause of srotodushti.
keyConcepts: Sroto Vimarsha - common features of vitiation
Ama as cause of srotas disorders
importantVerses: Srotas are innumerable, but 13 gross channels are clinically approachable.
Each of these channels has been described to possess a pair of base organs called mula.
Ama, the by-product of diminished agni, is the most common cause of srotodushti.

chapters.summary: This chapter deals with classification and categorization of diseases. It provides knowledge about different disease families, their characteristics and specific features. The chapter helps in understanding disease patterns and their management.

This chapter deals with examination of the diseased patient (Vyadhita). It provides detailed guidelines for patient assessment including physical examination, understanding patient's condition, and determining appropriate treatment approach based on the presentation of disease.

This chapter describes the qualities of an ideal teacher, medical student, and how to acquire medical knowledge. It provides guidelines for medical education including means to evaluate a medical treatise and ways to enhance medical knowledge by organizing medical conferences, group discussions and debates.

sthanas.description: Sharira Sthana deals with various aspects of human being - from origin of human beings to embryology, physiology, obstetrics, and neonatology, before delving into study of human anatomy.

chapters.summary: This chapter describes purusha (human being) in context of samyoga purusha (logical body of six constituents - shad-dhatuja), of twenty-four constituents (chaturvimshati-tattvatmak), or that which is ideal for treatment (chikitsya purusha). It deals with types of purusha, origin, constituents, details about mind and soul, process of knowledge, theory of evolution and destruction, types of diseases, treatment, and salvation.
importantVerses: Purusha comprises of six dhatu - five mahabhuta in subtle form and consciousness.
Purusha comprises of twenty-four dhatu - mind, ten indriya, five objects of sense organs and prakriti.
Ultimate reason for all kinds of pain is that human beings do not realize body and soul to be distinct.

chapters.summary: This chapter deals with units of reproduction and genetic principles. It covers aspects of beeja (seed/sperm), shonita (ovum), factors determining progeny, hereditary characteristics, and concepts of genetic inheritance in Ayurveda.

This chapter describes minor embryogenesis - the initial stages of fetal development. It covers month-wise development of embryo, formation of various body parts, and developmental milestones during pregnancy.

This chapter deals with major embryogenesis - detailed study of fetal development including formation of all body systems, organs, and tissues. It covers comprehensive month-wise development and factors affecting fetal growth.
This chapter provides comprehensive study of human being - physical, physiological and psychological aspects. It deals with detailed analysis of human body, mind, and their interrelationships.

This chapter deals with analytical study of body - definition of body, main factors for good health, equilibrium state, lifestyle and diet for maintenance. It includes discussion on which organ appears first during intra-uterine life and lifespan assessment.

This chapter covers anthropometry - number and measurements of body organs and structures. It includes description of skin (twak), six sections of body (shadanga), bones (asthi), sense organs (indriya), viscera (koshthanga), and various measurements including anguli pramana and anjali pramana.
importantVerses: Including teeth, teeth sockets and nails, human bones are 360 in number.
Quantity of rasa dhatu is nine anjalis, rakta is eight, mamsa is seven.
Water within whole body is equal to ten anjalis.

chapters.summary: This chapter deals with progeny and delivery - aspects of conception, pregnancy, childbirth and neonatal care. It covers garbhini paricharya (pregnancy care), prasuta paricharya (postpartum care), and jatamatra paricharya (newborn care).
